notes.meaning: Naomi wants to find Ruth a "resting place." She means a safe, settled home with a good husband who will care for her. Naomi had chosen to stay a widow herself, but she did not hold young Ruth to that choice. Henry sees a lesson here: parents should care about their children's future and seek what is truly good for them.

Naomi reminds Ruth that Boaz is a close relative. That makes him a "kinsman-redeemer." This was a family member whose duty was to protect his relatives, buy back family land, and marry a childless widow so the family name would go on. That night Boaz would be winnowing barley. Winnowing means tossing the grain into the evening breeze so the wind blows away the chaff. He would stay at the threshing floor all night to work and to guard his crop.

Naomi tells Ruth to wash, put on perfume, and wear her best clothes. Henry says she was to be clean and neat, not showy. Currid thinks this also showed that Ruth's time of mourning was over. Ruth was to wait until Boaz had finished his meal and was alone. That way her request would be private, and her good name would be safe if he said no.

Ruth was to lift the covering off Boaz's feet and lie down there, across the foot of his bed. Servants in that culture often slept like this at their master's feet. It was a custom of the day, not a sexual offer, and it was a humble way to remind Boaz of his duty as her kinsman-redeemer. Then he would tell her what to do. Henry and Clarke admit it looks risky to us. They say it worked only because Boaz was so godly, and it is not meant to be copied today.

Ruth agrees to do everything Naomi says. Henry notes that Ruth was too good and too sensible to promise this if she had seen anything wrong in it. He draws a lesson: younger people do well to follow the wise advice of their elders when they have no real reason to object.
Ruth goes down to the threshing floor and does just what Naomi told her. She watches where Boaz goes to lie down, as she was instructed.

Boaz "was in good spirits" after his meal. This means he was content and refreshed, not drunk. An old Jewish paraphrase says he blessed God for ending the famine. He slept by the grain pile to guard it. Ruth came quietly, lifted the covering from his feet, and lay down there, fully clothed.

At midnight Boaz wakes with a start. He leans over in the dark to feel who is there, and finds a woman at his feet. He clearly had no idea she was coming. Currid notes that his question "Who are you?" shows nothing improper was going on.

Ruth humbly calls herself his servant. "Spread the corner of your garment over me" was a way of saying "Marry me and protect me." She asks this because he is her kinsman-redeemer, the one with the right to carry on her late husband's family. Henry sees a picture here of how we can come to Christ, our close Relative, and ask for his care.

Boaz blesses Ruth. Her earlier kindness was her loyalty to her husband and to Naomi. Her new kindness is even greater. She did not chase younger men, rich or poor. Instead she turned to an older man so that her late husband's family could go on. She was not trying to improve her own life.

Boaz tells Ruth not to be afraid. He will do what she asks, because the whole town knows she is a woman of noble character. The same kind of words were used for Boaz himself in chapter 2. Henry notes that Ruth's goodness was well known even though she was poor.
Boaz is a kinsman-redeemer, but another man is a closer relative and has the first right. Naomi probably did not know this. Boaz could not act unless that man gave up his claim.

Boaz makes a solemn oath, "as surely as the LORD lives." If the closer relative will not redeem Ruth, Boaz will do it himself. He will speak to that man for her, so she does not have to. She should stay until morning, because walking back to town in the dark was not safe. The word used for "stay" here carries no sexual meaning.

Ruth lay at his feet, not by his side, until morning. She left before it was light enough for anyone to recognize her. Boaz wanted no one to know she had been there. This protected both their good names, and kept the closer relative's choice from being swayed. Henry's lesson: keep a good name as well as a clear conscience.

Boaz pours six measures of barley into Ruth's shawl. No one knows the exact amount, but it was probably as much as she could carry. The gift showed he was not sending her away in displeasure. Currid sees it as a pledge that Boaz would act soon. Then Boaz went into town.

Naomi's question is literally "Who are you, my daughter?" She is not unsure who Ruth is. She is eager to know what happened and whether Ruth comes home as a bride-to-be. Ruth tells her everything Boaz did.
Ruth shows Naomi the barley. Boaz did not want her to go home to Naomi empty-handed. The gift was kindness to poor Naomi, and a sign that Boaz was pleased with Ruth's request.

Naomi tells Ruth to wait quietly. Boaz will not rest until the matter is settled that very day. Ruth had done her part, and now she must trust and wait. Henry says believers can likewise leave their cares with God, who has promised to care for them.
